name: Lolegaon
tagline: A Lepcha ridge village with a walkway through the treetops
meta_description: Lolegaon (Loleygaon), Lepcha village at 1,675 m: heritage forest canopy walk, Jhandi Dara sunrise, Kafer view, WBFDC lodge, homestays, jeeps and costs.
summary: Lolegaon, also spelled Loleygaon, is a Lepcha village at 1,675 m on a ridge 24 km from Lava and 55 km from Kalimpong. It is known for the canopy walk through an old oak and cypress forest, the Jhandi Dara sunrise point and quiet homestays. One or two nights is enough.

local_story.title: The Lepcha ridge the forest corporation found
paras: Lolegaon is a Lepcha village. The Lepcha, who call themselves Rong, are the oldest known people of the Kalimpong and Sikkim hills, and their villages were here long before the Bhutanese, the British or the Nepali settlers who came later. Lolegaon's houses spread along a ridge at about 1,675 m, between Lava and the plains, with the old Kafer settlement and viewpoint about 1 km away. The 2011 census counted about 2,200 people in the village.

For most of the 20th century Lolegaon was a farming and forest village, reached on foot. That changed in the 1990s, when the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation set up tents and then cottages here, and Kolkata travellers discovered a cool, quiet ridge with a forest of huge old trees and a view of Kanchenjunga. The heritage forest, a patch of mossy oak and cypress kept from felling, became the village's showpiece when a hanging walkway of about 180 m was built through its canopy.
Lolegaon still feels like a village first. Homestays are run by local families, the forest is used for fodder and firewood as well as tourism, and in the evenings the ridge goes quiet early.

did_you_know: Lolegaon is also spelled Loleygaon and Lolaegaon; all three appear on road signs, maps and bookings.
The canopy walk in Lolegaon's heritage forest runs for about 180 m among old oak and cypress, several metres above the forest floor.
Lolegaon lies on NH717A, the newer road linking the Dooars with Lava and Pedong, built partly as an alternative to NH10.
intro: Lolegaon is a long, thin village on a forested ridge, with homestays spread out along the road and the heritage forest at its heart. Most visitors come for one night: a walk on the canopy bridge in the afternoon, Kanchenjunga at Jhandi Dara at dawn, and on to Lava or back to Kalimpong. Stay two nights and the village slows you down, which is the point.

It is cheap and simple. Homestays charge about ₹1,300–2,000 per person with meals, and the forest corporation's eco tourism centre is good value if you book ahead. There is little to buy and few places to eat outside your stay. Nights are cool, around 5–10 °C in winter, and the monsoon brings thick mist and leeches.
facts: Canopy walk, Jhandi Dara sunrise, Lepcha village
costs: Car to Jhandi Dara at dawn

highlights.title: Heritage forest canopy walk
highlights.text: A hanging walkway of about 180 m through the crowns of old oak and cypress trees draped with moss. Walk it slowly, early in the morning, and listen for birds. A small entry fee applies, and it closes in storms.

highlights.title: Jhandi Dara sunrise
highlights.text: A hilltop about 4–5 km from the village, named for its prayer flags (jhandi), where you watch the sun come up over Kanchenjunga. Book a car the night before or walk in the dark with a local guide.

highlights.title: Kafer viewpoint
highlights.text: About 1 km from the village, Kafer gives a wide Kanchenjunga view without the dawn effort. Late afternoon light on the range in October and November is good for photographs.

highlights.title: Lepcha village life
highlights.text: Lolegaon is a Lepcha village. Ask your host about Lepcha food, language and festivals such as Namsoong, and walk the lanes to see cardamom, maize and bamboo around the houses.

highlights.title: Forest birding
highlights.text: The heritage forest and the road towards Lava are good for laughingthrushes, barbets, sunbirds and woodpeckers. Early morning, before the day trippers arrive, is best.

how_to_reach.text: From NJP or Bagdogra a car costs about ₹4,500–6,000 and takes around 4 hours for roughly 124 km via Kalimpong and Lava, or via the Dooars and Gorubathan on NH717A. NH10 has had closures since October 2023, so check current status before you travel. From Lava, a car for the 24 km costs ₹1,800–2,500.

Take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Kalimpong (₹200–300), then from Kalimpong to Lava (₹120–180, mornings). Shared vehicles from Lava to Lolegaon are rare, so plan on a local car for the last leg. Allow a full day.
Charkhole is about 12–15 km away, 45 minutes to an hour by car (₹1,200–1,800). Many travellers combine the two Lepcha villages in one trip.

where_to_stay: Lolegaon has two choices. The forest corporation's Lolegaon Eco Tourism Centre, near the heritage forest, has simple rooms at about ₹2,000–3,000, booked on wbfdc.net, with meals cooked to order. Along the village road are family homestays run by Lepcha and Nepali households, at around ₹1,300–2,000 per person with dinner and breakfast; ask for one with a north-facing room for the Kanchenjunga view. There are no hotels, and very few restaurants, so your stay is also your kitchen.
tips: Walk the canopy bridge at opening time, before the day trippers from Lava arrive.
Book your Jhandi Dara car the night before; drivers start around 4.30–5.30 am depending on the month.
Carry cash; there is no reliable ATM and UPI depends on a patchy network.
Pack leech socks or long socks for forest walks from May to September.
The canopy walk can close for repairs or bad weather: check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Canopy walk in the heritage forest
experiences.summary: Walk about 180 m on a hanging bridge through the crowns of old, moss-covered oak and cypress in Lolegaon's heritage forest. Go early for birdsong and mist; it is the village's signature walk.
body: Lolegaon's heritage forest is a patch of old trees spared from felling: huge oaks and cypresses with trunks wrapped in moss, ferns and orchids. The canopy walk, a hanging bridge of wooden planks and steel cables, runs for about 180 m through their crowns, several metres above the forest floor. It moves a little under your feet, which is part of the fun.

Go at opening time, around 8 am, when the mist is still in the trees and the birds are busy. Walk slowly; stop at the platforms to look into the canopy for barbets, sunbirds and woodpeckers. Groups are asked to cross a few at a time, so be patient on busy weekends. Children love it, but keep a hand on small ones.

There is a small entry fee, and the bridge closes in storms and for maintenance. Afterwards, walk the trails at ground level among the same trees, which are just as impressive from below. In the monsoon, the forest is at its greenest and leeches are at their keenest.

faqs.q: How long is the Lolegaon canopy walk?
faqs.a: The hanging bridge is about 180 m long, through the crowns of old oak and cypress trees. Crossing takes 10–20 minutes at a slow pace, and most people spend an hour in the heritage forest including the ground trails.

faqs.q: Is the Lolegaon canopy walk safe for children?
faqs.a: Generally yes, for children who can walk steadily and with an adult holding them. The bridge sways a little and has side nets or rails. Follow staff instructions on group numbers. It is not suitable for people with a strong fear of heights.

faqs.q: What are the canopy walk timings?
faqs.a: It usually opens from morning to late afternoon, roughly 8 am to 4 pm, with a small entry fee. It can close in rain, wind or for repairs. Timings change, so check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Sunrise at Jhandi Dara
experiences.summary: Drive or walk 4–5 km in the dark to Jhandi Dara, the prayer-flag hilltop above Lolegaon, and watch Kanchenjunga light up at sunrise. The village's best hour, on a clear morning.
body: Jhandi Dara means 'flag ridge', after the prayer flags (jhandi) that cover it. It is a hilltop about 4–5 km from Lolegaon with an open view north-west to the Kanchenjunga range and the hills of Sikkim. At dawn, the peaks catch the sun while the valleys are still full of cloud.

Book a car with your homestay the night before; it costs about ₹600–1,000 return. You leave about 45 minutes before sunrise, so around 5 am in October and March and closer to 5.30 am in December and January. Some guests walk up with a torch and a local guide, which takes about an hour each way. Wrap up warmly: it is often close to freezing at dawn in winter.

October to early December gives the best odds of a clear sky, with February to April a good second. If the peaks are hidden, wait 20–30 minutes; cloud often parts briefly after sunrise. Come back to the village for breakfast and the canopy walk.

faqs.q: How far is Jhandi Dara from Lolegaon?
faqs.a: About 4–5 km, 15–20 minutes by car on a narrow road, or an hour on foot. A car for the sunrise trip costs about ₹600–1,000 return. Book it with your homestay the evening before.

faqs.q: Can you see Kanchenjunga from Jhandi Dara?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings. The view to the north-west takes in the Kanchenjunga range above the hills of Sikkim. The best chances are from October to early December and February to April. From June to September, the peaks are usually hidden.

faqs.q: What should I carry for Jhandi Dara sunrise?
faqs.a: A warm jacket, cap and gloves in winter, a torch, water and a flask of tea if your homestay will make one. Wear shoes with grip, because the hilltop path can be wet with dew. Carry a camera with a zoom lens for the peaks.

experiences.title: Kafer viewpoint and a Lepcha village walk
experiences.summary: Walk about 1 km to the Kafer viewpoint for an afternoon view of Kanchenjunga, then wander back through the village lanes with a local guide, past Lepcha and Nepali houses, cardamom and bamboo.
body: Kafer, about 1 km from the centre of Lolegaon, is the older part of the village and its easiest viewpoint. In the late afternoon of a clear autumn day, the Kanchenjunga range turns gold above the valley. You do not need to get up at dawn for it, which makes it popular with families and older travellers.

The walk there and back is the real reward. Ask your host or a local guide to take you through the lanes rather than along the road. You pass houses with kitchen gardens of squash and chillies, cardamom growing in the shade, stands of bamboo, and small shrines. Lepcha and Nepali families live side by side; ask about the Lepcha language and Namsoong, the Lepcha New Year in December or January.

Be a good guest: greet people, ask before photographing anyone or entering a yard, and do not hand out sweets to children. A local guide costs about ₹500–800 for two or three hours and is the easiest way to be welcomed.

faqs.q: Where is Kafer in Lolegaon?
faqs.a: Kafer is about 1 km from the centre of Lolegaon, easy to reach on foot along the village road or lanes. It has an open view of the Kanchenjunga range, best in the late afternoon from October to December and in spring.

faqs.q: Is Lolegaon a Lepcha village?
faqs.a: Yes. Lolegaon is a Lepcha village, though Nepali families also live there. The Lepcha, or Rong, are the oldest known inhabitants of the Kalimpong and Sikkim hills, with their own language, script and festivals such as Namsoong, the Lepcha New Year.

faqs.q: Can I find a local guide in Lolegaon?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask your homestay or the forest lodge staff. A village guide costs about ₹500–800 for a two- or three-hour walk, more for a dawn walk to Jhandi Dara. Specialist bird guides are rarer; book them through Lava or Kalimpong in advance.

experiences.title: An evening in a Lepcha homestay kitchen
experiences.summary: Spend dinner time in your host family's kitchen: squash and ferns from the garden, fermented greens, rice, pickles and perhaps a Lepcha dish, with stories about the village told around the fire.
body: In Lolegaon, as in most hill villages, the kitchen is the warmest room in the house and the centre of family life. Ask your hosts if you can join them while dinner is cooked. Depending on the season, the meal might include squash and its tender shoots, ningro fern tips in spring and the monsoon, mustard greens, radish, local dal, rice and a sharp tomato or chilli pickle.

Many Lepcha households also cook dishes from their own tradition, and ingredients from the forest, such as wild greens and bamboo shoots, appear in season. Ask what is Lepcha and what is Nepali on your plate; families often cook both. Gundruk, fermented and sun-dried greens made after the autumn harvest, turns up in soups and pickles in winter.

Do not expect a cooking class or a fixed menu. This is a family meal, and the conversation matters as much as the food. Offer to help, wash your own plate if it is the custom, and thank the cook. If you have dietary needs, tell your hosts when you book.

faqs.q: What food is served in Lolegaon homestays?
faqs.a: Home-cooked Nepali and Lepcha meals: rice, dal, seasonal vegetables such as squash, ferns and greens, pickles, eggs, and chicken on request. Breakfast is often puri-sabzi, bread and eggs or noodles. Meals are usually included in the homestay rate of about ₹1,300–2,000 per person.

faqs.q: What is Lepcha food like?
faqs.a: Lepcha cooking uses rice and maize, wild greens, ferns, bamboo shoots, mushrooms and fermented foods, often lightly spiced. Many dishes are steamed or boiled. In homestays you will usually get a mix of Lepcha and Nepali home food; ask your hosts which dish is which.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians eat well in Lolegaon?
faqs.a: Yes. Most homestay meals are vegetable-based: dal, rice, squash, greens, potatoes and pickles, with eggs or chicken only on request. Tell your hosts in advance if you are vegetarian or avoid eggs, onion or garlic, and they will usually adapt.

faqs.q: Is Lolegaon worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for a quiet night or two. Lolegaon has the canopy walk through an old forest, the Jhandi Dara sunrise over Kanchenjunga and the calm of a Lepcha ridge village. It is cheap and uncrowded outside weekends. If you want shopping, restaurants or nightlife, it is not for you.

faqs.q: How far is Lolegaon from Kalimpong?
faqs.a: About 55 km via Algarah and Lava, a 2.5–3 hour drive. A reserved car costs ₹3,000–4,000 one way. Shared jeeps run from Kalimpong to Lava, but rarely beyond, so plan on a car for the last 24 km.

faqs.q: Lolegaon, Loleygaon or Lolaegaon: which is right?
faqs.a: All three spellings are used for the same village, along with variants on hotel sites and road signs. Wikipedia uses Loleygaon. If you are searching for homestays or the forest lodge, try each spelling to find all options.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Lolegaon?
faqs.a: One night covers the canopy walk, Kafer and a sunrise at Jhandi Dara. Two nights give you a second chance at a clear dawn and time for a village walk or a trip to Charkhole. Combine it with two nights at Lava or Kolakham.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Lolegaon?
faqs.a: October to December for clear Kanchenjunga views, and March to May for flowers, birds and mild weather. January and February are cold but often clear. From June to September it is wet and misty, with leeches in the forest, but very green.

faqs.q: Is Lolegaon good for families?
faqs.a: Yes. The canopy walk is a hit with children, distances within the village are short and homestays are welcoming. Choose a homestay with an attached bathroom and hot water, keep the Jhandi Dara dawn for older children, and carry warm clothes for evenings.

faqs.q: Can I go from Lolegaon to Siliguri directly?
faqs.a: Yes. Cars can go down via Lava and Gorubathan to the Dooars and Siliguri, or via Kalimpong on NH10. Allow about 4 hours. Ask your driver which road is open, because NH10 has had frequent closures since October 2023. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM in Lolegaon?
faqs.a: Do not count on one. Withdraw cash in Kalimpong or Siliguri for homestays, cars and entry fees. UPI works where the mobile network is good, which in Lolegaon is patchy. Small notes are useful for entry fees and tea stalls.

faqs.q: Lolegaon or Lava: where should I stay?
faqs.a: Stay in Lava for the monastery, Neora Valley access and better jeep links; stay in Lolegaon for the canopy walk, Jhandi Dara and a more village feel. They are 24 km apart, about an hour by car, and many travellers spend one or two nights in each.
